blocks.body:
The rotations of three-dimensional space form a group: composing two rotations gives a rotation, and every rotation can be undone. But this group is not a list of elements like a finite group. A rotation is described by an axis and an angle, three real parameters in all, and nearby rotations differ only slightly. The group is at the same time a smooth three-dimensional space on which one can do calculus.

Sophus Lie's idea, in the 1870s, was to study such continuous groups of symmetries through their infinitesimal versions, much as calculus studies a curve through its tangent lines. A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with the group operations smooth. Most examples are groups of matrices cut out by polynomial equations: rotation groups, unitary groups, the groups of matrices with determinant $1$. They are the symmetry groups of geometry and of physics. This page assumes [[groups]] and [[smooth-manifolds]] (charts, smooth maps, tangent spaces and the regular value theorem).

blocks.title: Lie group
blocks.body:
A Lie group is a group $G$ that is also a smooth manifold, such that multiplication $G \times G \to G$, $(g,h) \mapsto gh$, and inversion $G \to G$, $g \mapsto g^{-1}$, are smooth maps. A Lie group homomorphism is a group homomorphism that is also a smooth map. The dimension of $G$ is its dimension as a manifold.

So a Lie group is a group in which one can differentiate, and the algebra and the geometry are compatible.

blocks.title: Examples, and matrix groups
blocks.body:
Simple examples: $(\mathbb{R}^n, +)$; the circle $S^1 = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| = 1\}$ under multiplication; the torus $S^1 \times S^1$; any finite or countable group with the discrete topology (a $0$-dimensional Lie group).

The main family consists of matrix groups. The general linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ of invertible real $n \times n$ matrices is an open subset of the space $M_n(\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ (it is where $\det \ne 0$), hence a manifold of dimension $n^2$. Matrix multiplication is polynomial in the entries and inversion is rational (Cramer's rule), so both are smooth. Inside it sit
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R}) &= \{A : \det A = 1\}, \\
\mathrm{O}(n) &= \{A : A^{\mathsf T}A = I\} \quad \text{(maps preserving lengths)}, \\
\mathrm{SO}(n) &= \{A \in \mathrm{O}(n) : \det A = 1\} \quad \text{(rotations)},
\end{aligned}$$
and, with complex entries and conjugate transpose $A^*$, the unitary groups $\mathrm{U}(n) = \{A : A^*A = I\}$ and $\mathrm{SU}(n) = \{A \in \mathrm{U}(n) : \det A = 1\}$. Each is a subgroup defined by polynomial equations in the entries (real and imaginary parts, in the complex case), so it is a closed subset. The next theorem shows these are submanifolds, and computes their dimensions.

blocks.title: Orthogonal and special linear groups are Lie groups
blocks.body:
$\mathrm{O}(n)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ of dimension $n(n-1)/2$, with tangent space at the identity
$$T_I\,\mathrm{O}(n) = \{X \in M_n(\mathbb{R}) : X^{\mathsf T} + X = 0\}.$$
$\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ is an embedded submanifold of dimension $n^2 - 1$ with $T_I\,\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R}) = \{X : \operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$. Both are Lie groups. Similarly $\dim \mathrm{SO}(n) = n(n-1)/2$, $\dim \mathrm{U}(n) = n^2$ and $\dim \mathrm{SU}(n) = n^2 - 1$.

Let $\mathrm{Sym}_n$ be the space of symmetric matrices, of dimension $n(n+1)/2$, and define $F\colon M_n(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{Sym}_n$ by $F(A) = A^{\mathsf T}A$. Then $\mathrm{O}(n) = F^{-1}(I)$. Expanding $$F(A + tX) = A^{\mathsf T}A + t(X^{\mathsf T}A + A^{\mathsf T}X) + t^2 X^{\mathsf T}X$$ shows
$$dF_A(X) = X^{\mathsf T}A + A^{\mathsf T}X.$$
For $A \in \mathrm{O}(n)$ this is onto $\mathrm{Sym}_n$: given symmetric $S$, put $X = \tfrac12 AS$; then $X^{\mathsf T}A + A^{\mathsf T}X = \tfrac12 S A^{\mathsf T}A + \tfrac12 A^{\mathsf T}AS = S$. So $I$ is a regular value, and by the regular value theorem $\mathrm{O}(n)$ is an embedded submanifold of dimension $n^2 - n(n+1)/2 = n(n-1)/2$, whose tangent space at $I$ is $\ker dF_I = \{X : X^{\mathsf T} + X = 0\}$.

For $\mathrm{SL}_n$, use $\det\colon M_n(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$. For invertible $A$, $$\det(A + tX) = \det A \det(I + tA^{-1}X) = \det A\,(1 + t\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}X) + O(t^2))$$, so $d(\det)_A(X) = \det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}X)$, which is onto $\mathbb{R}$ (take $X = cA$). Hence $1$ is a regular value, $\dim \mathrm{SL}_n = n^2 - 1$, and $T_I\,\mathrm{SL}_n = \{\operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$.

In each case the group operations are restrictions of the smooth operations of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ to an embedded submanifold, so they are smooth. $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ is the open and closed subset of $\mathrm{O}(n)$ where $\det = +1$ (the determinant of an orthogonal matrix is $\pm 1$), so it has the same dimension. For $\mathrm{U}(n)$ the same argument with Hermitian matrices (real dimension $n^2$) inside $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ (real dimension $2n^2$) gives $\dim \mathrm{U}(n) = n^2$, and $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ is cut out of it by one more real equation.

blocks.title: Closed subgroups and homogeneity
blocks.body:
More generally, Cartan's closed subgroup theorem (stated here without proof) says that every closed subgroup of a Lie group is an embedded submanifold, hence itself a Lie group. So any closed subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ or $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is a Lie group; these are the matrix Lie groups. The proof uses the exponential map of the next page, [[lie-algebras]].

Two features make Lie groups far more rigid than general manifolds. First, for each $g$ the left translation $L_g(h) = gh$ is a diffeomorphism of $G$ (with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$) carrying the identity $e$ to $g$. So a Lie group looks the same near every point, and all of its local structure is visible at $e$. In particular its tangent space $\mathfrak{g} = T_eG$ determines a great deal; equipped with a bracket coming from the group law, it is the Lie algebra of $G$. Second, connectivity spreads local information everywhere, as the next theorem shows.

blocks.title: A connected group is generated by any neighbourhood of the identity
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a connected Lie group (more generally, a connected topological group) and $U$ any neighbourhood of the identity. Then every element of $G$ is a finite product of elements of $U$.

Choose an open set $W$ with $e \in W \subseteq U$ and let $V = W \cap W^{-1}$, an open set containing $e$ with $V^{-1} = V$ and $V \subseteq U$, and let $H = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} V^n$, where $V^n$ is the set of products of $n$ elements of $V$. Then $H$ is a subgroup: it is closed under products, and under inverses because $(v_1\cdots v_n)^{-1} = v_n^{-1}\cdots v_1^{-1}$ with each $v_i^{-1} \in V$.

$H$ is open: for $h \in H$, the set $hV$ is open (left translation is a homeomorphism), contains $h$, and lies in $H$. Its complement is open too, being the union of the cosets $gH$ with $g \notin H$, each open for the same reason. So $H$ is nonempty, open and closed, and connectedness of $G$ gives $H = G$.

blocks.title: Example 1: the circle group
blocks.body:
Show that $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ consists exactly of the rotation matrices
$$R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix},$$
that $\theta \mapsto R_\theta$ is a Lie group homomorphism $(\mathbb{R}, +) \to \mathrm{SO}(2)$ with kernel $2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, and that $\mathrm{SO}(2) \cong \mathrm{U}(1) = S^1$.
blocks.solution:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ with $A^{\mathsf T}A = I$ and $\det A = 1$. The columns are orthonormal, so $(a, c)$ is a unit vector, $(a,c) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ for some $\theta$. The second column is a unit vector orthogonal to the first, so $(b, d) = \pm(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, and $\det A = \pm(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = \pm 1$ forces the $+$ sign. So $A = R_\theta$; conversely every $R_\theta$ is in $\mathrm{SO}(2)$.

The addition formulas for sine and cosine are precisely the statement $R_\theta R_\varphi = R_{\theta + \varphi}$, so $\theta \mapsto R_\theta$ is a homomorphism; it is smooth, and $R_\theta = I$ exactly when $\theta \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. Finally $R_\theta \mapsto e^{i\theta}$ is a well-defined bijective homomorphism onto $\mathrm{U}(1) = \{z : |z| = 1\}$ (it is multiplication by $e^{i\theta}$ on $\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}^2$), smooth with smooth inverse. All three groups are the circle.

blocks.title: Example 2: SU(2) is a 3-sphere and covers SO(3) twice
blocks.body:
Show that
$$\mathrm{SU}(2) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & -\overline{b} \\ b & \overline{a} \end{pmatrix} : a, b \in \mathbb{C},\ |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1 \right\},$$
so that $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is diffeomorphic to the $3$-sphere $S^3 \subset \mathbb{C}^2 = \mathbb{R}^4$. Then describe the homomorphism $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathrm{SO}(3)$ and its kernel.
blocks.solution:
The form. A unitary matrix has orthonormal columns. If the first column is $(a, b)$ with $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, the second column is a unit vector orthogonal to it, so it is $\lambda(-\overline{b}, \overline{a})$ with $|\lambda| = 1$ (the orthogonal complement of $(a,b)$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is the line through $(-\overline{b}, \overline{a})$). The determinant is $\lambda(|a|^2 + |b|^2) = \lambda$, so $\det = 1$ forces $\lambda = 1$. Conversely every such matrix is unitary with determinant $1$. The map to $(a, b) \in S^3$ is a diffeomorphism. In particular $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is connected and simply connected.

The covering of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the real $3$-dimensional space of traceless Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices
$$X = \begin{pmatrix} z & x - iy \\ x + iy & -z \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det X = -(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).$$
For $U \in \mathrm{SU}(2)$ the map $X \mapsto UXU^{-1}$ preserves $\mathcal{H}$ and preserves the determinant, so it is a linear map of $\mathbb{R}^3$ preserving $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$, an element of $\mathrm{O}(3)$. This gives a smooth homomorphism $\Phi\colon \mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathrm{O}(3)$; as $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is connected and $\det \Phi(U) = \pm 1$ varies continuously, the image lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. The kernel consists of the $U$ commuting with every element of $\mathcal{H}$, hence (since $\mathcal{H}$ together with $I$ spans all complex $2 \times 2$ matrices) with every matrix, so $U$ is a scalar of determinant $1$: $U = \pm I$. One can show (we omit the proof) that $\Phi$ is onto, so
$$\mathrm{SO}(3) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)/\{\pm I\} \cong S^3/(\text{antipodal map}) = \mathbb{RP}^3 .$$
Topologically, $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is not simply connected: its [[fundamental-group|fundamental group]] is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. This is the mathematics behind spin in quantum mechanics.

blocks.title: Example 3: every rotation of space has an axis
blocks.body: (Euler's rotation theorem.) Prove that every $A \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ has a fixed axis: there is a unit vector $v$ with $Av = v$.
blocks.solution:
We show $\det(A - I) = 0$. Using $A A^{\mathsf T} = I$,
$$\det(A - I) = \det(A - AA^{\mathsf T}) = \det A \cdot \det(I - A^{\mathsf T}) = \det\big((I - A)^{\mathsf T}\big) = \det(I - A).$$
For $3 \times 3$ matrices $\det(I - A) = (-1)^3\det(A - I)$. So $\det(A - I) = -\det(A - I)$, hence $\det(A-I) = 0$, and $1$ is an eigenvalue: some unit vector $v$ satisfies $Av = v$. The plane $v^\perp$ is mapped to itself, and $A$ acts on it by an element of $\mathrm{SO}(2)$, a rotation by some angle (Example 1). So every element of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a rotation about an axis, which confirms the count of three parameters: two for the axis direction and one for the angle.

The same argument works in every odd dimension; in even dimensions it fails, e.g. $-I \in \mathrm{SO}(2)$ fixes no nonzero vector.

blocks.title: Topology, compactness, and where Lie groups appear
blocks.body:
Connected components. $\mathrm{O}(n)$ has two components, $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ and the reflections with $\det = -1$; $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ also has two, according to the sign of the determinant; $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathrm{SL}_n$, $\mathrm{SO}(n)$, $\mathrm{U}(n)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ are connected.

Compactness. $\mathrm{O}(n)$, $\mathrm{U}(n)$ and their closed subgroups are compact (closed and bounded in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ or $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, since every column is a unit vector). The rest of this section states standard theorems without proof. A compact Lie group carries a Haar measure, an invariant probability measure, so one can average over it exactly as one averages over a finite group. Consequently Maschke's theorem from [[group-representations]] holds for continuous finite-dimensional representations of compact groups, and the Peter–Weyl theorem extends Fourier series from the circle to every compact Lie group.

Rigidity. A continuous homomorphism between Lie groups is automatically smooth, and the solution of Hilbert's fifth problem (Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin, 1952) shows that every topological group that is locally Euclidean admits a Lie group structure. Smoothness is forced by the group structure.

Physics. $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is the symmetry group of a rotationally invariant system, and by Noether's theorem this symmetry corresponds to conservation of angular momentum. The Lorentz group $\mathrm{O}(1,3)$ of matrices preserving $t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2$ is the symmetry group of special relativity, and the gauge group of the Standard Model is $\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)$.

- Not every Lie group is a matrix group: the universal cover of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ has no faithful finite-dimensional representation. Matrix groups are the main examples, not the definition.
- A subgroup that is a nice curve need not be a Lie subgroup in the embedded sense. In the torus $S^1 \times S^1$ the subgroup $\{(e^{it}, e^{iat}) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ with $a$ irrational is dense, not closed, and not an embedded submanifold.
- Count real dimensions: $\mathrm{U}(n)$ consists of complex matrices but has real dimension $n^2$; it is not a complex submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb{C})$.
- $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ look the same near the identity (both are $3$-dimensional with the same tangent structure) but are not isomorphic: one is simply connected, the other has fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

The tangent space at the identity, with the bracket inherited from the group law, is the subject of [[lie-algebras]], where the exponential map $X \mapsto e^X$ connects it back to the group. Representations of compact Lie groups extend [[group-representations]] and [[character-theory]], and for the circle they reduce to [[fourier-series]]. Lie groups acting on manifolds give the homogeneous spaces of [[riemannian-geometry]], such as spheres $S^{n-1} = \mathrm{SO}(n)/\mathrm{SO}(n-1)$, and their topology is studied with [[fundamental-group]] and [[homology]]. The underlying point-set notions are on [[topological-spaces]].

1. The symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, \mathbb{R}) = \{A : A^{\mathsf T}JA = J\}$, where $J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_n \\ -I_n & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, is a Lie group. Imitate the proof for $\mathrm{O}(n)$ to show that its dimension is $n(2n+1)$.
2. Show that $\det\colon \mathrm{U}(n) \to \mathrm{U}(1)$ is a surjective Lie group homomorphism with kernel $\mathrm{SU}(n)$, and deduce $\dim \mathrm{SU}(n) = n^2 - 1$ again.
3. Show that $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is not compact, and that $\mathrm{O}(n)$ is compact.
4. Find an element of $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ that fixes no nonzero vector of $\mathbb{R}^4$.
